title: Top Down Operator Precedence (chapter 9 of Beautiful Code)
version: chapter 9 of Beautiful Code, dated 2007-02-21; viewed 2026-10-13
why: Crockford's JavaScript account of Pratt's method, which defines nud, led and binding powers and the infix/infixr associativity trick.

title: Pratt Parsers: Expression Parsing Made Easy
why: Nystrom's widely read 2011 reintroduction of Pratt parsing, useful for the popularisation history and for the parselet presentation.

title: Simple but Powerful Pratt Parsing
why: Kladov's minimal Pratt parser, the clearest account of left/right binding-power pairs and how they encode associativity.

title: Pratt Parsing and Precedence Climbing Are the Same Algorithm
why: Chu's argument and evidence that precedence climbing and Pratt parsing are one algorithm.

title: Parsing Expressions by Recursive Descent
version: © 1999 with later updates (deriving section dated 2013); viewed 2026-10-13
why: Norvell's account of the recursive-descent and precedence-climbing expression parsers, and his note on who invented and named precedence climbing.

claim: Pratt presented the paper "Top Down Operator Precedence" at the first annual Principles of Programming Languages Symposium in Boston in 1973.
quote: Vaughan Pratt presented "Top Down Operator Precedence" at the first annual Principles of Programming Languages Symposium in Boston in 1973.

claim: In Crockford's account, a nud (null denotation) does not look at the tokens to the left and is used by values and prefix operators, while a led (left denotation) does look left and is used by infix and suffix operators.
quote: A nud does not care about the tokens to the left. A led does. A  nud method is used by values (such as variables and literals) and by prefix operators. A led method is used by infix operators and suffix operators.

locator: header, below the title and the byline dated 2007-02-21
claim: Crockford's article on top-down operator precedence is chapter 9 of the book Beautiful Code.
quote: This is chapter 9 of Beautiful Code.

locator: section 'Peanut butter and jelly, the secret weapon', third paragraph
claim: Nystrom writes that Crockford's JSLint uses a Pratt parser and that Crockford's treatment was one of the very few remotely modern articles about it.
quote: Douglas Crockford’s JSLint uses one to parse JavaScript, but his treatment is one of the very few remotely modern articles about it.

locator: section 'Infix Operators', the infixr helper calling expression(bp - 1)
claim: Crockford's ordinary infix operators are left associative, and right-associative operators such as the short-circuiting logical operators are made by reducing the right binding power.
quote: Those infix operators are left associative. We can also make right associative operators, such as short-circuiting logical operators, by reducing the right binding power.

locator: section 'Minimal Pratt Parser', numbered note 3 after expr_bp
claim: In Kladov's Pratt loop, an operator's left binding power is compared against the current minimum and its right binding power becomes the minimum for the recursive call on its right operand.
quote: Note how we use l_bp to check against min_bp, and r_bp as the new min_bp of the recursive call. So, you can think about min_bp as the binding power of the operator to the left of the current expressions.

claim: Chu concluded, after implementing both, that precedence climbing and Pratt parsing are the same algorithm.
quote: In doing so, I realized that Precedence climbing and Pratt parsing are the same algorithm.

locator: closing notes just before the References list
claim: Norvell writes that neither Keith Clarke nor Martin Richards gave the algorithm a name, and that he suggested the name "precedence climbing".
quote: Neither Clarke nor Richards had a special name for the algorithm, so my one contribution (besides extending it to postfix and non-associative operators) is suggesting the name "precedence climbing".
